turns_text: [SEG0001] person_1 (NURSE): right, before you start, blood pressure today is 152 over 84, pulse 72. last time it was 164 over 90, just so you've got it.
[SEG0002] person_2 (PATIENT): that's fine though. I feel alright. bit of a waste of a morning if you ask me.
[SEG0003] person_3 (DOCTOR): mm. and the bloods I asked for this morning, can you read me the kidney ones?
[SEG0004] person_1 (NURSE): yeah. creatinine is 174, eGFR 34. back in the spring the eGFR was 41.
[SEG0005] person_3 (DOCTOR): thanks. so this is your diabetes and kidney review. how have you been in yourself?

[SEG0006] person_2 (PATIENT): I'm fine. err, they just sent the letter for the kidney thing. bit of an ache in the knee, few months, nothing really. comes on if I walk to the shops, goes when I sit down.
[SEG0007] person_4 (CAREGIVER): he wouldn't have come if I hadn't pushed. my sister's been on dialysis three years now, and I can't stop thinking about it.
[SEG0008] person_2 (PATIENT): oh leave off. I'm not like that. I'm fine.
[SEG0009] person_3 (DOCTOR): you've got type 2 diabetes, and the chronic kidney disease we've been following. still on the ramapril, and the metformin?

[SEG0010] person_2 (PATIENT): yeah both by mouth. ramipril five milligrams in the morning, metforman for the sugar, five hundred twice a day. diabetic fifteen years. the kidneys, they told me a couple of years back.
[SEG0011] person_3 (DOCTOR): anything from the shop, for pain?
[SEG0012] person_2 (PATIENT): just ibuprofen. four hundred milligram tablet, by mouth, when the knee niggles. not every day. hardly worth mentioning.
[SEG0013] person_4 (CAREGIVER): Mm. he gets them by the till at the shop. I did say.
[SEG0014] person_3 (DOCTOR): I'd rather you weren't on those with these kidneys. any chest pain?
[SEG0015] person_2 (PATIENT): no.
[SEG0016] person_3 (DOCTOR): and breathlessness, walking about?
[SEG0017] person_2 (PATIENT): not really.
[SEG0018] person_3 (DOCTOR): any vomiting?
[SEG0019] person_2 (PATIENT): never.
[SEG0020] person_3 (DOCTOR): with the diabetes, any numbness or tingling in the feet?
[SEG0021] person_2 (PATIENT): no.
[SEG0022] person_3 (DOCTOR): getting thirsty, drinking more?
[SEG0023] person_2 (PATIENT): not that either. well, actually, a bit in the evenings. nothing much.
[SEG0024] person_3 (DOCTOR): up in the night to pass water?
[SEG0025] person_2 (PATIENT): no... well, sometimes. just the once.
[SEG0026] person_3 (DOCTOR): and your bowels, any trouble there?
[SEG0027] person_2 (PATIENT): yeah, fine. no trouble.
[SEG0028] person_3 (DOCTOR): let me check. ankles are soft, no swelling. the knee isn't hot, and it isn't swollen.

[SEG0029] person_3 (DOCTOR): so, just to say it back. mild ache in the knee for a few months, worse on walking, eases when you sit. shop ibuprofen now and then, ramipril five milligrams, metformin five hundred twice a day, type 2 diabetes for fifteen years, kidney disease a couple of years. today the pressure is 152 over 84, creatinine 174, eGFR 34.

[SEG0030] person_3 (DOCTOR): I think the ibuprofen has nudged the kidney function down, on top of the kidney disease we already know about. that's my working impression, not the final word. the repeat bloods will tell us more.

[SEG0031] person_3 (DOCTOR): the way it works, ibuprofen narrows the little vessels into the kidney filters, and ramipril drops the pressure on the way out, so together they can push the creatinine up. and diabetes can dull the nerves in the feet, which is why I asked about the tingling, even though you're not getting that.
[SEG0032] person_4 (CAREGIVER): so those tablets go in the bin? I had a stomach ulcer myself years ago from ibuprofen, I won't touch the stuff.

[SEG0033] person_3 (DOCTOR): yes, please stop the ibuprofen, don't buy any more. we'll keep the ramipril at five milligrams, that's for your blood pressure and the kidneys. metformin stays at five hundred twice a day while your eGFR is above 30. for the knee, paracetemol by mouth, one gram up to four times a day.
[SEG0034] person_2 (PATIENT): paracetamol doesn't do anything. uh, fine, if you say so. the ibuprofen was barely anything anyway.
[SEG0035] person_3 (DOCTOR): I'll book repeat kidney bloods in two weeks, creatinine and the eGFR again. if those haven't settled we might arrange a kidney ultrasound, but not just yet.
[SEG0036] person_3 (DOCTOR): I'll see you back here in six weeks with the results. if the knee gets properly worse before that, come sooner.
[SEG0037] person_1 (NURSE): I'll sort the blood form at the desk. mind the step on the way out.

spec.situation: Older diabetic with kidney disease on review; creatinine and eGFR read aloud; takes ibuprofen from a shop against advice; ramipril continued, painkiller advice changed.

traps.happens: The doctor (or nurse) explains a mechanism or a diagnosis in the patient's body ('the voice box is irritated by reflux', 'diabetes dulls the nerves in the feet', 'the swelling is your body fighting infection'). A nurse or caregiver also mentions a fact about THEIR OWN life (their sister, their child, their own illness).
traps.label_rule: Explanations by the doctor are NEVER symptoms, history or social history of the patient; they may only appear as clinical_assessment or counselling if the doctor stated them as such. A nurse's or caregiver's own life facts are not recorded as the patient's. Each symptom's reported_by is the person who really described it.

traps.happens: The patient denies some symptoms (said as 'no', 'not really', 'never'), has a chronic condition named earlier (for example asthma or hypertension) and later the doctor asks about another symptom of it, and one answer is a double negative or a correction ('not that either', 'no... well, sometimes').
traps.label_rule: Denials go in negative_findings with the exact thing denied, never in symptoms. NEVER write a negative about a condition the patient has said they have. A corrected answer keeps only the final version. A negative is never a symptom, and 'not painful' is the finding 'pain' absent, not a symptom called 'painless'.

features: hedged_plan: the doctor hedges ('we might do a scan if it does not settle', 'let's see in two weeks'). Conditional vs planned status must follow the words.
doctor_misses_topics: the doctor does not ask about everything; topics never discussed are simply absent (no invented denials, no allergy line if allergies were never mentioned).

bad.reason: Evening thirst is reported, but certainty isn't certain: patient hedges 'actually, a bit' and 'nothing much'.
bad.text: evening thirst (category=endocrine, status=present, severity=mild, frequency=in the evenings, temporality=current, reported_by=patient, certainty=certain)

bad.reason: Nocturia reported sometimes once nightly, but certainty isn't certain: patient first says 'no... well, sometimes'.
bad.text: nocturia (category=genitourinary, status=present, frequency=sometimes, once a night, temporality=current, reported_by=patient, certainty=certain)

bad.text: chronic kidney disease (status=existing, duration=a couple of years, reported_by=doctor)
